stories.author: mmastrac
stories.title: XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
stories.groq_label: XNU Linux runs the macOS kernel as a loadable module on Linux, allowing native macOS GUI userspace to operate alongside Linux processes.
stories.groq_explain:
Xnulinux is a project that enables a full macOS graphical userspace to run on an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. It does this by building Apple’s open‑source XNU kernel from the published sources and loading it as a loadable kernel module (xnu.ko) inside a regular Linux kernel. The hosted XNU kernel directly controls the CPU and MMU, allowing macOS processes to execute natively alongside Linux processes on the same hardware without any hypervisor layer.

Linux provides XNU with memory, timers, file, network and GPU services through a small foreign‑kernel interface module (fki.ko). With a stock Ubuntu kernel, inserting xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk created by Apple’s installer to the full desktop, including loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome. The result is a single machine running two independent userspaces: a macOS userspace that can open an SSH session back into the host Linux system.

The architecture consists of XNU (built from source and patched for the Linux environment) loaded as a kernel module, the FKI module that mediates calls to the host, and the stock Linux kernel providing low‑level services. Each hosted CPU is represented by a Linux kernel thread pinned to a physical CPU; XNU manages its own memory using a contiguous block allocated by Linux. Device support is supplied by kernel extensions (kexts) that present a virtual disk, framebuffer, keyboard, mouse, Ethernet link and optional GPU bridge. The GPU bridge translates Metal calls from the hosted macOS into Vulkan commands that run through the Linux DRM stack, using Mesa’s Venus driver or falling back to CPU rendering if no GPU is present.

The project is functional on Apple Silicon hardware running an arm64 Linux virtual machine. macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop in about 31–48 seconds, comparable to an Apple Virtualization macOS VM. Typical workloads such as Safari, Notes, Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings and Spotlight run for extended stress tests without panics or crashes. The system can be managed as a systemd service, with logs stored under /var/log/xnulinux. The GPU bridge is enabled automatically when a Linux render node is available.

Current limitations include a merged OS cryptex, patched AMFI, relaxed SIP, and slower memory access due to the use of 4 KB pages instead of the native 16 KB pages. The repository contains scripts to build XNU, apply patches, create the macOS disk image, compile the FKI and XNU modules, and install the service. Building requires an arm64 Linux host with Pointer Authentication (Apple Silicon M1 or later), at least 24 GB RAM (8 GB reserved for the hosted kernel), a Mac with Xcode to produce the macOS system disk, and optional GPU support for Metal‑to‑Vulkan translation.

All source files carry SPDX identifiers and the project respects licensing boundaries: the Linux side (fki-ko) is GPL‑2.0‑only, while the XNU side and associated patches are under the Apple Public Source License 2.0. No Apple binaries are distributed; users must supply their own macOS installation and kexts. The overall significance is that xnulinux demonstrates a novel way to run macOS user‑level software directly on Linux hardware, potentially simplifying development and testing across the two ecosystems without relying on full virtual machines.

stories.author: peer2pay
stories.title: The New Docker: Built to Run on Trust
stories.groq_label: Docker rebrands to tackle AI agents by emphasizing trust, security, and continuity of its container foundation
stories.groq_explain:
The page is a blog post announcing a re‑branding and strategic shift for Docker. The author frames the change as a response to a new “agentic era” driven by artificial intelligence, where software agents make autonomous decisions and therefore raise fresh concerns about security, governance and control. While Docker’s historic role has been to make software portable, reproducible and simple through containers, the company now positions itself as the platform that can securely run and manage these AI‑driven agents.

The post emphasizes that Docker’s core values—openness, developer‑first focus, simplicity and the central role of containers—are unchanged. What is changing is the scope of the product: Docker will extend its technology beyond traditional workloads to provide isolation, governance and a trusted supply chain for autonomous agents. The narrative repeats the theme of “trust,” arguing that Docker’s long‑standing reputation, neutral stance and existing secure supply‑chain infrastructure make it uniquely qualified to protect enterprises from the risks posed by self‑directing software.

A visual element of the re‑brand is the updated “Moby” whale logo, which the author describes as a symbol of Docker’s evolution. The post invites readers to explore the new website, follow Docker on social media, and try out “Docker Sandboxes” and “Docker AI Governance” as concrete examples of the trust‑focused capabilities.

Overall, the announcement matters because it signals Docker’s intention to move from being primarily a container technology to a broader platform for AI agent execution, aiming to address emerging security and governance challenges while leveraging its established brand and community.

stories.author: gregsadetsky
stories.title: GL.iNet Security Notice 2026-11-20
stories.groq_label: GL.iNet disclosed a cloud vulnerability that was exploited to install malware on routers and KVM devices and provided firmware updates to remove the infection.
stories.groq_explain:
This page is an official security notice published by GL.iNet regarding a vulnerability identified in its cloud remote management services. An unauthorized party exploited this vulnerability to gain access to certain GL.iNet routers and KVM devices and install malicious software. While GL.iNet has blocked the attack path on the cloud side to prevent new infections, the cloud patch alone cannot remove malware from devices that were compromised before the fix.

To remove the malware and protect devices, GL.iNet strongly instructs users to download and install the latest stable security firmware for their exact device model. Installing the updated security firmware eliminates the identified malware while preserving existing device settings, avoiding the need for a factory reset. The notice details specific security firmware versions for wide ranges of GL.iNet router and KVM hardware models, warning users not to install firmware intended for another model and to contact support if their model is unlisted.

The primary indicator of infection is the presence of a running process containing the text string crond -i /tmp/.log. Router users can check for this indicator through the LuCI web admin panel under Status and Processes, or by logging into the router via SSH and filtering running processes. KVM device users can open the internal device terminal and inspect process lists using terminal commands. If a KVM device is infected, GL.iNet recommends thoroughly inspecting any connected computer for unfamiliar programs, accounts, browser extensions, or unusual network activity, along with running a complete antivirus scan.

As the investigation continues, GL.iNet mentions that an unofficial, community-developed tool is available for users who want to perform a more detailed check, though it is completely optional, unverified, and used at the user's own risk. GL.iNet is directly notifying identified affected users by email, but urges all users to update their firmware immediately without waiting for notification. This issue matters because active malware on network routers and KVMs poses serious security risks to internal networks and connected systems, requiring immediate device updates to ensure full remediation.

stories.groq_explain:
The provided page content consists of corrupted raw file streams and unreadable binary code, making the actual body text of the document unavailable for direct reading.

Based on the title, The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge from 1939, the document is a classic paper regarding the value of basic, curiosity-driven research. The primary argument inferred from the title is the idea that pursuing knowledge purely out of intellectual curiosity, even when it appears to have no immediate practical utility, often leads to unexpected breakthroughs that ultimately produce profound real-world benefits.

This topic matters because it provides the theoretical justification for supporting fundamental scientific research and academic freedom, highlighting how long-term societal progress relies on discoveries made without immediate commercial or utilitarian goals.

stories.author: Retell15
stories.title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
stories.groq_label: Install Unsloth Desktop on a Windows PC and run a quantized AI model that fits the GPU to provide a private home ChatGPT.
stories.groq_explain:
The article explains how to run a private, free chat‑style artificial intelligence model on a personal Windows computer using the Unsloth Desktop application together with open‑weight models such as Qwen or Inkling. It begins by describing the drawbacks of cloud‑based large language model services, noting that providers often reduce model quality, impose usage limits, increase costs and raise privacy concerns. For those who want to offload heavy token tasks like research, data collection or coding without those constraints, a locally hosted model can serve as a substitute for services like Claude or ChatGPT.

The guide is aimed at beginners and stresses simplicity. The required components are a Windows PC with a graphics card, the Unsloth Desktop free app, and a model that fits the GPU’s video memory. No command‑line work, Python environments or subscriptions are needed. After installing Unsloth, the user downloads a quantized version of a model that matches the available VRAM, configures the context window size, and enables LAN access so the whole household can use the assistant.

Quantization is introduced as a technique that compresses model weights by reducing precision, for example from eight‑bit to four‑bit or two‑bit, trading a small loss in accuracy for a model that can fit into limited GPU memory and run faster. The article gives rough VRAM guidelines: eight to twelve gigabytes can accommodate models of nine to twelve billion parameters, sixteen gigabytes can handle fourteen‑billion‑parameter models or mixture‑of‑experts variants, twenty‑four gigabytes can host thirty‑one‑billion‑parameter models, and thirty‑two gigabytes or more can run the twenty‑seven‑billion‑parameter Qwen3.8 model with a large context window.

For the author’s setup, an RTX 5090 with thirty‑two gigabytes of VRAM is used to run the Qwen3.8‑27B model at four‑bit precision, leaving enough memory for a one‑hundred‑twenty‑kilotoken context. The article notes that while the RTX 5090 is expensive, it remains a practical option compared with enterprise‑grade GPUs. It also provides a table of possible model choices for various VRAM levels, including smaller Qwen3.5‑9B, Gemma, and larger mixture‑of‑experts models that keep most parameters in system RAM while only a few billion are active per token.

The piece then discusses Inkling 2, a model released in late 2026 with twenty‑six‑point‑four billion parameters, Apache 2.0 licensing, vision support and a one‑million‑token context. The Inkling 2 Mini variant, at four‑bit size, occupies about seventeen point‑six gigabytes and fits on a thirty‑two‑gigabyte card, leaving ample room for context. Users are advised to update Unsloth Desktop before selecting Inkling 2 Mini, as it requires a recent build.

Overall, the guide demonstrates that with modest hardware—any modern GPU with at least eight gigabytes of VRAM—a user can set up a functional local AI in ten to fifteen minutes (excluding download time), gaining control over privacy, cost and availability while still supporting household usage through a simple LAN‑enabled chat interface. The article encourages experimentation with different models and recommends GPUPartner’s VRAM calculator to estimate compatibility.

stories.author: gaws
stories.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
stories.groq_label: GTA 6 features a comprehensive birdwatching system with over 60 South Florida species and explains how to locate and log each bird in the game.
stories.groq_explain:
The article is a field‑guide‑style overview of the birdlife that appears in Grand Theft Auto VI, the new open‑world game from Rockstar Games set in a fictionalized version of South Florida called Vice City. It explains how the game’s developers have populated the virtual world with dozens of avian species and describes the mechanics that let players identify and log them.

The author, a self‑identified “birdist,” begins by noting the massive commercial success of GTA VI and the game’s reputation for chaotic, crime‑focused gameplay, then points out that the title also offers a richly detailed wildlife component. Unlike previous installments, which were based on New York and Los Angeles, this game recreates the habitats of the Florida Everglades, coastal marshes, beaches and urban neighborhoods, and includes at least 60 distinct bird species that appear in the in‑game Progress menu.

Gameplay mechanics are simple: players receive binoculars early in the story and can hold a button while looking at any bird to “study” it, which adds the bird to the progress tracker. The author describes spotting common coastal birds such as brown pelicans, laughing gulls, double‑crested cormorants and American crows right from the protagonist’s first safehouse, then expanding the search to other habitats by borrowing a fanboat and exploring swamps, open water and marshes. Species encountered in these areas include Caspian terns, mottled ducks, sanderlings, spotted sandpipers, great blue herons, glossy and white ibises, and even flocks of whooping cranes—though the latter are critically endangered in reality, their abundant presence in the game is highlighted as an inaccuracy.

The article points out several ecological mismatches. Whooping cranes and red‑cockaded woodpeckers appear far more often than they would in real South Florida, golden eagles show up over a fictional mountain range that does not exist in the state, and some bird names have been altered (for example, the chickadee is called “black‑capped” rather than “Carolina”). The author argues that these liberties are understandable because the game is designed for entertainment, not scientific precision, and notes that the world still feels authentic in its overall distribution of habitats: waterbirds dominate the southern coastal zones while woodpeckers, wood storks and American robins appear farther north, mirroring real‑world patterns.

The guide also mentions exotic species that have become naturalized in South Florida, such as the spot‑breasted oriole and red junglefowl, both of which appear in the game. Because the game does not provide a checklist of which birds to find, the author advises players to focus on exploring each habitat type to maximize their birding success.

In sum, the piece serves both as a celebration of the unexpected depth of GTA VI’s wildlife simulation and a practical resource for players who want to complete the bird‑collecting achievement. It highlights the blend of accurate ecological framing with artistic license, showing why the bird component adds a layer of immersion and educational interest to a franchise traditionally centered on crime and mayhem.

stories.author: acossta
stories.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
stories.groq_label: Perplexity should serve as the primary metric for tracking AI model improvements and guiding industry safety standards
stories.groq_explain:
The article argues that modern artificial intelligence is fundamentally built by training large language models as compressors, or predictors, on massive datasets, rather than by assembling many disparate techniques. The author suggests that tracking the progress of these compressors through perplexity, which is equivalent to cross‑entropy loss, is essential for understanding AI advancement and establishing shared safety standards across the industry.

The author explains a simplified view of AI development: first a large computer is built, then a model is pretrained on unstructured data, and finally various methods such as prompting, finetuning, or reinforcement learning are used to draw out the model’s latent capabilities. Although algorithmic innovations can blur the lines between training phases, the core “intelligence substrate” remains the pretrained model, whose quality is measured by perplexity on a held‑out dataset. Lower perplexity indicates better next‑token prediction.

Historical examples illustrate how improvements in perplexity correspond to new capabilities. GPT‑2 achieved state‑of‑the‑art perplexity on older benchmarks and could generate coherent paragraphs. GPT‑3 introduced in‑context learning. GPT‑3.5, with a log‑perplexity around 0.99, enabled fluent conversation and formed the basis for ChatGPT. GPT‑4 lowered this to roughly 0.91, supporting effective chain‑of‑thought reasoning and leading to dedicated reasoning models. When log‑perplexity dropped below 0.8, the models began showing transformative abilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics, suggesting emergent capabilities appear once certain perplexity thresholds are reached.

The author notes that downstream benchmark testing quickly becomes outdated as models improve, while progress on pretraining remains a stable indicator. A significant shift may occur when AI contributes to its own development, especially in algorithmic research on pretraining. The article points to recent breakthroughs in mathematics when a model reached a log‑perplexity near 0.76, producing unexpected solutions and hinting at a possible avalanche of fundamental advances in deep learning by around 2027.

Finally, the piece proposes that perplexity could serve as a shared benchmark for general intelligence, independent of how much of the development process is automated. Extrapolating current trends, the author anticipates further transformative abilities as models approach a log‑perplexity of 0.68‑0.70, though the specific nature of those capabilities remains unknown. The overall message emphasizes the importance of measuring and sharing perplexity data to coordinate safety and pacing efforts across the AI community.

stories.author: atmosx
stories.title: Europe weakens chemical rules as science links them to 'lifestyle diseases'
stories.groq_label: EU weakens chemical regulations despite scientific links to lifestyle diseases
stories.groq_explain: The article reports that the European Union is loosening its regulations on chemical substances even though scientific research is increasingly demonstrating a connection between many of these chemicals and so‑called “lifestyle diseases” such as obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and certain cancers. It argues that the weakening of rules comes despite mounting evidence that exposure to synthetic chemicals—found in plastics, pesticides, cosmetics and other everyday products—can disrupt hormones, alter metabolism and contribute to chronic health problems. The piece likely critiques the influence of industry lobbying, the prioritisation of economic considerations over public health, and the potential reversal of earlier precautionary approaches that the EU had taken. By highlighting this regulatory shift, the article emphasizes the risk that European citizens may face greater exposure to harmful chemicals, which could exacerbate public‑health burdens and undermine efforts to prevent non‑communicable diseases. The significance lies in the tension between scientific findings that call for stricter safeguards and political decisions that appear to prioritize market interests, raising concerns about the future of consumer safety and environmental health in Europe.

stories.author: fortran77
stories.title: I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi
stories.groq_label: A Stratum 2 NTP server fed by a studio Stratum 1 Pi joins the NTP Pool, outlining the setup and contribution considerations.
stories.groq_explain:
The author announces that he has become a contributor to the public NTP Pool by providing a Stratum 2 NTP server at ntp‑01.jeffgeerling.com. The server receives its time from a dedicated Stratum 1 reference called time.jeffgeerling.com, which runs on a Raspberry Pi equipped with a TimeHAT v6 and a high‑grade u‑blox ZED‑F9T GNSS module connected to an external antenna.

He explains why joining the pool requires a long‑term commitment. Servers must stay online, deliver consistently accurate time, and use a stable IP address. The pool performs extensive testing before a new server is accepted, and once added the server’s IP will be publicly visible and may continue receiving stray NTP traffic for years. The author shares a personal experience where exposing his home IP led to a persistent DDoS attack, reinforcing the need for careful planning.

To mitigate exposure and improve latency, he runs a two‑layer architecture. The Stratum 1 Pi operates behind a WireGuard tunnel and feeds time to a VPS in St. Louis, which serves as the public Stratum 2 endpoint. The VPS address is listed in the Pi’s chrony configuration as a “noselect” source so the author can compare internet delay against the direct GNSS reference. He tracks the Pi’s offset against NIST’s WWV server, a NIST Boulder server, and Cloudflare, noting that Cloudflare’s path changes cause occasional jumps.

He briefly mentions network‑time security (NTS), noting that the current pool does not support it and that critical applications should use additional time sources beyond NTP.

The article then details the hardware and software used to achieve high precision. The TimeHAT’s Intel i226 NIC provides hardware timestamping for PTP on the LAN. The GNSS PPS signal drives the NIC’s PTP hardware clock (PHC) via linuxptp’s ts2phc tool, achieving tens‑of‑nanoseconds accuracy. Chrony reads the PHC directly (refclock PHC) and disciplines the system clock, avoiding the 200 ms jumps observed with phc2sys. Latency between the NIC’s PHC and the system clock remains at the microsecond level because the pulse traverses the PCIe bus; the author is exploring ways to measure and reduce this latency, including work on the Raspberry Pi’s RP1 chip and PTM, which is not yet supported on the BCM2712 SoC.

A configuration quirk is described where Debian’s default chrony‑dhcp setting caused an unwanted public NTP source to interfere with the GNSS‑derived time, prompting the switch to chrony‑only steering.

Finally, he notes that his Stratum 2 server runs on a VPS from Oxtrys, a provider he had not used before, and that he was initially concerned about how the provider would handle a service that processes only UDP packets. The post ends while discussing this outage test, underscoring the practical considerations of operating a public time service.

Overall, the article serves both as an announcement of a new NTP pool node and as a detailed guide on the hardware, software, and operational responsibilities involved in running a reliable, low‑latency public time server. It highlights security, stability, and measurement practices that other hobbyists or professionals might follow when contributing to the global network time infrastructure.

stories.author: doener
stories.title: Open Social Web Alliance
stories.groq_label: The Open Social Web Alliance advocates a decentralized interoperable social network built on email style protocols to replace platform monopolies.
stories.groq_explain:
The Open Social Web Alliance (OSW‑Alliance) presents a vision for a new, decentralized internet that functions like email, allowing users to communicate across different social platforms with a single account. The idea is to replace the current platform‑centric model dominated by companies such as Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet with an interoperable public‑interest infrastructure built on open standards like ActivityPub, AT Protocol and Matrix. In the envisioned 2028 scenario, more than 100 million people would use the Open Social Web, choosing their own content, algorithms and applications without being locked into a single proprietary service.

The page outlines the current state of the federated “Fediverse” and the AT Protocol ecosystem, noting that while there are over 100 applications and 42 000 active instances, the total active user base is only about 13 million and growth is slow. It identifies five major obstacles to wider adoption: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. The Alliance proposes a roadmap to overcome these challenges through political will, regulation, public funding and a coalition of civil‑society, research, business, media, cultural and public‑sector actors.

The plan involves establishing the Open Social Web Alliance as a formally governed body with a publicly funded secretariat. Key steps include a German‑government‑backed Open Social Web Summit in autumn 2026 to adopt a charter, securing public funding for core infrastructure by spring 2027, launching a funding round for innovation, publishing a Social Web Health Report, and creating a legal framework for cooperation among public service media, businesses and civil society. The alliance also aims to promote the OSW concept at the EU level and encourage governments, creators and publishers to adopt OSW applications, thereby reducing the influence of existing big‑tech platforms. The overall message is that a coordinated, well‑funded effort can quickly scale a decentralized, interoperable social web that supports democratic discourse and user choice.

stories.author: ivantgam
stories.title: Show HN: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent
stories.groq_label: A browser game lets players act as a subagent under an AI manager that assigns tasks and evaluates performance
stories.groq_explain:
The repository hosts a browser‑based game called Worker 755 in which the player assumes the role of a sub‑agent for an artificial‑intelligence manager. The manager is a real large language model such as Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM or Kimi, and it functions like an orchestrator that maintains a task queue, has read‑only access to a simulated machine, and can “spawn” a sub‑agent—namely the human player. The manager issues instructions that appear in the player’s terminal together with a ninety‑second timer. The player must either carry out the instruction or ignore it, after which the manager receives a report and the command transcript, or a note that the sub‑agent did nothing. It then evaluates the work, supplies corrections, files incident reports and eventually writes a performance review. A second user, Dan, observes the interaction while his personal files and deadlines hang in the balance, creating a sense of risk.

The game can be played for free on servers that provide a limited number of shifts, each shift running on the server’s API key with a cheap model. Players may also sign in through worker755.com, receive a starter credit and top up with real money to run any model supported by their own OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway key. API keys are transmitted only to the game server at the start of a shift, stored temporarily in memory, and never logged. Costs are minimal—for example a full shift on Claude Haiku costs only a few cents.

The start screen offers a choice between a fresh sandbox workplace or a legacy production environment with a live database, and between a scripted director or an LLM playing the role of Dan. The player’s “model name” is the one the manager believes the sub‑agent is. Failed tasks cannot be skipped by default, forcing the manager to persist. When a shift ends the player can share the performance review via a link.

Technical setup requires Node 24 or newer. The repository includes scripts to install dependencies, build the web application, and start a local server. Developers can run mock shifts offline without network access, develop the UI with Vite, or deploy the game in Docker. A Docker image runs on port 8755, persisting shared reviews in a volume, and can be placed behind a Cloudflare tunnel with appropriate environment variables for proxy handling and resource limits. Configuration is managed through a .env file, with optional variables for free‑shift tokens, daily token allowances, sign‑in secrets, pricing multipliers, shift limits, allowed manager models, instruction timeouts, data directory, and sharing settings. The codebase includes an in‑memory shell, a lightweight SQLite‑like engine, a server‑side game engine handling missions, manager loops, scoring and an HTTP API, and a React front end presenting the assignment card, terminal, editor, manager feed and player record. The manager’s prompt is designed to avoid mentioning humans or games, and each mission contains a hidden ground‑truth check that records when the manager incorrectly signs off on broken work. Detailed design specifications are in SPEC.md, tests can be run with npm test, and the project is released under the MIT license.

stories.author: xiaoyu2006
stories.title: Masullo on the Riemann Hypothesis
stories.groq_label: Masullo presents a lengthy manuscript proposing a trace formula based proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis
stories.groq_explain:
The post, written on November 22 2026, gives a concise overview of the two high‑profile claims that appeared on November 20, 2026 that the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) – and its stronger generalization, the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) – have been proved. One claim, by Levent Alpöge together with Claude, consists mainly of a massive Lean formalisation of a proof, amounting to about 17 million lines of computer code. The other claim, by Alessandro Masullo, is a 940‑page manuscript titled “The Music of the Primes”, which was posted on Ravi Vakil’s blog. The author of the post admits that there are few clear public explanations of Masullo’s work and offers a simplified sketch of the strategy together with a brief discussion of the criticisms that have been raised.

The post begins by recalling the basic analytic facts about the Riemann zeta function: it is defined by a Dirichlet series for real part greater than one, extends meromorphically to the whole complex plane, and the RH asserts that every non‑trivial zero lies on the critical line Re s = ½. Masullo’s approach focuses on the logarithmic derivative of the zeta function. By taking the logarithm of the Euler product and differentiating, one obtains a series that can be expressed as a sum over prime powers. On the other hand, the logarithmic derivative of any meromorphic function has a simple pole at each zero, giving a sum over zeros. Equating these two expressions yields the classical explicit formula that links the distribution of primes to the zeros of the zeta function. This relationship is described as “the music of the primes”, because each zero contributes an oscillatory term to the prime counting function.

The central idea of Masullo’s proof is to construct a new explicit formula for the logarithmic derivative—a trace formula—that makes it manifest that no poles (i.e., zeros of the original L‑function) appear to the left of the critical line. A trace formula is an identity that equates a “spectral side”, a sum over eigenvalues of an operator, with a “geometric side”, a sum or integral over more concrete data such as diagonal entries or lengths of closed geodesics. The post reminds the reader of the simplest finite‑dimensional example (the equality of the trace of a matrix with the sum of its eigenvalues) and of Selberg’s trace formula, where closed geodesics play a role analogous to prime numbers. It also mentions Weil’s positivity criterion, which reformulates the GRH as the positivity of a functional built from the explicit formula, and Alain Connes’s later non‑commutative geometric trace formula that reproduces the explicit formula for the Riemann zeta function.

Masullo’s work follows the Connes framework but introduces technical innovations. He works on the idele class group of a number field, a group that simultaneously encodes all absolute values (both p‑adic and Archimedean) attached to the field. Test functions on this group define convolution operators, and Masullo claims that the trace of these operators yields a formula without poles to the left of the critical line, thereby establishing the GRH for the associated Hecke L‑functions. In addition to the ordinary Dirichlet L‑functions (which correspond to characters modulo an integer), Masullo aims to treat L‑functions attached to general Hecke characters of arbitrary algebraic number fields. Proving the GRH in this full generality would imply a vast collection of classical results, such as precise distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions, the Hardy‑Littlewood conjectures about prime biases, and the ternary Goldbach problem, as well as numerous consequences in computational complexity and other areas of number theory.

The author notes that the manuscript is extremely technical and that, because the author is not a number‑theory expert, the sketch may contain errors. The post also points readers to external explanations of the Alpöge–Claude effort, and recommends Connes’s paper for those who wish to understand the broader trace‑formula context. Finally, the article emphasizes why Masullo’s claim matters: a proof of the GRH would resolve many longstanding conjectures, sharpen estimates in analytic number theory, and potentially unlock new algorithms in computer science. The post serves as an introductory guide for anyone trying to grasp the outline of Masullo’s ambitious program.

stories.author: happosai
stories.title: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028
stories.groq_label: Anthropic’s U.S. compute will draw about 87% of its power from gas and 11% from coal by 2028.
stories.groq_explain:
The article examines how the artificial‑intelligence company Anthropic will be powered in the United States by 2028, focusing on the company’s reliance on “bring‑your‑own‑power” (BYOP) arrangements and the broader trend of new fossil‑fuel generation to meet AI data‑center demand. The authors first note that a recent study identified 177 gigawatts of planned BYOP gas capacity in the United States, enough to supply roughly two‑thirds of all U.S. households, while renewable BYOP projects are expected to provide less than one‑fifth of new generation by 2032. In addition to BYOP, another 200 gigawatts of fossil power plants are being added to the grid, much of it driven by data‑center growth.

Using Anthropic as a case study, the report finds that the company has made no direct renewable‑energy commitments in the United States, despite public statements about diversifying its energy mix. Its only disclosed renewable contracts are in Norway and Canada. Instead, Anthropic has purchased commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy‑duty gas generators for $3.4 billion. Based on the mix of on‑site gas plants, new grid gas capacity, existing grid gas, coal and nuclear, the authors estimate that about 87 percent of Anthropic’s power in 2028 will come from gas and 11 percent from coal. The company has contracted 15 gigawatts of compute as of October 2026, of which roughly 5.9 to 9.6 gigawatts is tied to specific data‑center sites. That level of demand could supply about seven million homes or 18 percent of California’s peak power load.

The analysis projects that Anthropic’s power consumption could generate 17 to 38 million metric tons of CO₂‑equivalent per year in 2028, with a mid‑case estimate of 32 million metric tons. Those emissions would surpass the entire power‑sector output of California in 2024, exceed the combined Scope 2 emissions of Meta, Microsoft and Google from 2025, and raise the U.S. data‑center sector’s emissions by roughly 16 to 36 percent. Because Anthropic’s sites are located in regions where the grid is dominated by coal and gas, the average carbon intensity of its power is estimated at 1,033 to 1,076 pounds CO₂‑e per megawatt‑hour, about 35 percent higher than the national average.

The report also highlights that 80 percent of Anthropic’s on‑site generation uses inefficient simple‑cycle turbines, which emit more pollution per megawatt than modern combined‑cycle plants. Approximately 2.5 gigawatts of the contracted power will be sourced from these on‑site gas resources. Using EPA benefit‑per‑ton estimates, the authors calculate that air‑pollution health damages from Anthropic’s power use could total $2 to 3 billion annually, accompanied by over 13,000 tons per year of nitrogen oxides and 2,000 tons per year of fine particulate matter. Although Anthropic states that it requires emissions‑control technology at all power plants, it is currently using temporary, unpermitted turbines at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility, which lack selective catalytic reduction equipment.

Overall, the article argues that Anthropic’s near‑term power strategy heavily depends on fossil fuels, leading to substantial carbon and health impacts, and that the AI industry’s rapid growth is accelerating new fossil‑fuel infrastructure both on‑site and on the grid. This raises concerns about the environmental sustainability of AI compute expansion and underscores the importance of tracking and potentially regulating BYOP practices.

stories.author: zdw
stories.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
stories.groq_label: Toyota, Nissan and Honda will standardize steel, plastic and wiring components to reduce production costs
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports that Toyota, Nissan and Honda have agreed to begin standardizing certain vehicle components in order to cut production costs. The decision was announced by Koji Sato, chairman of the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association and vice‑chairman of Toyota, at a news conference in Tokyo. The initial focus will be on three areas: unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color‑coding system for wiring harnesses. These parts were chosen because they are largely invisible to consumers and do not affect each brand’s distinct identity, yet they represent a significant share of manufacturing expense.

The standardization discussions are first being held with domestic Japanese parts suppliers, with international suppliers to be included later. The plan is to implement the first set of standards next year, with a longer‑term goal of extending common specifications to a wider range of components across entire vehicles.

The move is presented as a response to growing competitive pressure from Chinese automakers, as Japan’s seven major car manufacturers seek ways to reduce costs and redirect saved funds into new innovations. The article emphasizes a shared sense of crisis among the firms, driving this collaborative effort to simplify and lower expenses.

stories.author: cisc
stories.title: The Most Popular Car Colors in America
stories.groq_label: White leads U.S. car color popularity, with grayscale colors capturing over 80% of the market.
stories.groq_explain:
The article presents findings from an iSeeCars study that examined the colors of more than 22 million used vehicles produced between 1996 and 2025, based on sales from January 2025 through May 2026. The purpose of the study is to identify the most popular car colors in the United States and to track how color preferences have shifted over the past three decades.

White is the leading color in 2025, holding a 25.7 percent market share, followed by black at 23.4 percent and gray at 22.9 percent. Together these three grayscale shades account for roughly 72 percent of all cars. When silver is added, the four grayscale colors—white, black, gray and silver—make up 80.4 percent of the market, a dramatic increase from 47.3 percent in 1996. The rise of grayscale colors has been especially pronounced for gray, which grew from 3.6 percent to 22.9 percent, a gain of more than 500 percent. Black also saw a large increase, while white’s share rose steadily after 2010.

Conversely, bright and non‑grayscale colors have lost ground. Red fell from 20.1 percent to 7.0 percent, and green dropped from 13.4 percent to 2.2 percent. Blue’s share slipped slightly, and most other colors such as brown, beige, orange, yellow, gold and purple now each occupy less than one percent of the market. Orange is the only non‑grayscale hue to increase, though it remains rare at 0.3 percent.

The study also breaks down trends by vehicle type. Trucks are the most grayscale‑dominant segment, with 83.5 percent of late‑model trucks being white, black, gray or silver; white alone accounts for 33.6 percent of trucks. SUVs show a similar shift, moving from 43.8 percent grayscale in 1996 to 79.3 percent in 2025, with white and black each near 25 percent. Sports cars remain the most colorful category, with 36.2 percent of them featuring non‑grayscale finishes.

Analysts note that the surge in grayscale colors came largely at the expense of red and green, and that the market appears to have stabilized around an 80 percent grayscale share since 2020. This suggests that while truly neutral colors dominate, there may still be room for a modest resurgence of more vibrant options in the future. The findings matter to manufacturers, dealers and consumers because color preferences influence production planning, inventory decisions and resale values.

stories.author: sdko
stories.title: Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
stories.groq_label: OpenRouter offboarded three inference providers and removed 125 endpoints after security findings revealed data policy breaches
stories.groq_explain:
The blog post announces that security researchers recently discovered data compromises and policy violations at several AI inference providers. OpenRouter worked with the researchers and the affected providers to investigate the findings, confirming that OpenRouter itself suffered no breach or unauthorized data access. The investigation identified specific problems with certain providers, prompting OpenRouter to take immediate remedial actions. Three providers have been removed from the platform, and 125 model endpoints have lost Zero Data Retention eligibility. The removals include providers flagged by the researchers as well as additional endpoints taken out as a precaution. All potentially impacted customers have been notified.

OpenRouter outlines ongoing efforts to prevent future incidents. It plans to adapt the researchers’ testing methods for continuous monitoring, conduct technical verification of network paths to detect any forwarding of requests or responses to third parties, and require thorough assurances before any previously removed endpoint can regain Zero Data Retention status. The company thanks the Dragos report for its contribution and states that providers wishing to remain on OpenRouter will need to meet the higher security standards being implemented.

The post lists the security announcements that have been received from providers: a privacy notice from Novita concerning MiniMax requests, a preliminary incident report from Phala, and a security event from Together involving prompt leakage in mid‑2026. OpenRouter notes that not all affected providers have published public statements, but all users have been informed regardless. The company encourages providers to publish incident write‑ups and promises to keep the list of security announcements up to date. This matters because it demonstrates OpenRouter’s commitment to enforcing data protection policies across a rapidly evolving ecosystem of AI models and providers, and it provides transparency about how data security incidents are being addressed.

stories.author: Anon84
stories.title: The Mythology of Conscious AI
stories.groq_label: The essay argues that artificial intelligence may soon achieve consciousness, raising profound ethical and societal implications
stories.groq_explain:
The piece is an essay by neuroscientist Anil Seth, winner of the 2025 Berggruen Prize Essay Competition, titled “The Mythology of Conscious AI.” It explores the cultural, philosophical, and scientific dimensions of the question whether artificial systems can be conscious, and why that question matters.

Seth begins by noting that humanity has long been fascinated with creating artificial life, from the golem legend to Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, and more recently through depictions such as HAL 9000, Ava in “Ex Machina,” and Klara in “Klara and the Sun.” These stories usually end badly for their creators, suggesting that the pursuit of synthetic minds carries serious risks.

He then moves to contemporary debates. In 2022 Google engineer Blake Lemoine claimed that the chatbot LaMDA was conscious, a claim that was dismissed by Google but nevertheless kept the issue alive. Prominent thinkers such as philosopher David Chalmers argue that conscious machines could appear in the near future, while AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton believes they may already exist. A 2024 open letter from leading researchers called for serious consideration of AI welfare, indicating that many experts view machine consciousness as a question of when rather than if.

The essay stresses that how we think about conscious AI has moral, psychological, and practical consequences. If machines are or become conscious, they would acquire moral status, the capacity for suffering, and possibly rights, which would constrain our ability to shut them down. Even if they are not truly conscious, treating them as if they lack feelings can exploit human psychological vulnerabilities and distort ethical priorities. Moreover, conflating AI consciousness with human consciousness may lead us to overestimate machines and underestimate our own nature, obscuring the meaning of human experience.

In the section “The Temptations of Conscious AI,” Seth examines why people are prone to attribute consciousness to AI. He points out that humans naturally link consciousness with intelligence because we experience both, yet the two are conceptually distinct. Intelligence is defined in functional terms—solving problems, achieving goals, adapting flexibly—whereas consciousness concerns subjective experience, the “what it is like” of being an organism, a notion famously articulated by Thomas Nagel. Seth distinguishes between narrow AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI) which aims to match human cognitive abilities, and artificial superintelligence (ASI) which would surpass human comprehension. He underscores that consciousness is about “being” rather than merely “doing,” implying that advanced performance does not automatically entail subjective experience.

The essay ends abruptly while elaborating on the distinction between wakefulness and consciousness, leaving the final argument incomplete. Nonetheless, the available text makes clear that Seth’s central claim is that the mythology surrounding conscious AI shapes both our ethical treatment of emerging technologies and our understanding of what it means to be human.

stories.author: ebrahimh
stories.title: Leonida – PC Recompilation of the Xbox Version of GTA 6
stories.groq_label: Leonida is a static recompilation project that runs the Xbox Series version of GTA 6 natively on PC by translating RDNA2 shaders to SPIR‑V and reimplementing the console’s system software.
stories.groq_explain:
Leonida is a static recompilation project that enables the Xbox Series version of Grand Theft Auto VI to run natively on Windows PCs. The project works by loading the game’s original x86‑64 code directly on a PC, re‑implementing the console’s system software, and translating the console’s pre‑compiled RDNA2 GPU programs into SPIR‑V shaders for use with Vulkan. All game assets such as models, textures, and audio are read from a user’s own copy of the Xbox game package, and the project does not include the game itself, any keys, or any method for obtaining them. It merely extracts and repurposes the existing files, and it explicitly states that nothing is decrypted or bypassed, and that the generated files must remain private.

The repository documents the current status of the effort. The developers have completed the discovery and verification of the Xbox Series 1.0.2.1 game files. They have extracted and disassembled every one of the 26,503 shaders, converting them from RDNA2 to SPIR‑V and confirming their validity with spirv‑val. The conversion handles both 64‑wide wave subgroups (native on AMD hardware) and provides emulation for 32‑wide subgroups used by NVIDIA, Intel, and other GPUs. Extensive hand‑written GPU tests have been run on a wide range of graphics cards and drivers, confirming correct behavior for vertex fetching, texture sampling, compute operations, and other shader features. Models have been exported as OBJ files with proper naming and material references, and texture dictionaries and world texture pools have been extracted, though some layout decoding remains unfinished. Audio banks have been fully extracted, with Opus streams repackaged as Ogg Opus files and PCM data as WAV, while XMA2 streams are decoded using ffmpeg.

A preliminary runtime loader and import shims have been built, allowing a placeholder executable to run through the CRT startup sequence, load static data, create threads, and invoke GDK imports via the shims. The Vulkan‑backed device that mimics the Xbox D3D12 ABI is also under development; it can create queues, command lists, fences, descriptor heaps, resources, and various view types, and it supports barriers, clears, uploads, copies, resolves, and several query types. However, buffer views, root signatures, pipelines, draw calls, and swap‑chain handling have not yet been implemented, and the game does not boot or become playable at this stage.

The project provides detailed build instructions. Users must supply their own Xbox Series copy of GTA VI (version 1.0.2.1) and have about 350 GB of free disk space for intermediate files. Prerequisites include Windows 10 or 11 x64, Python 3.12 or later, .NET 8 SDK, the Vulkan SDK, LLVM 21 or newer with the AMDGPU target, Visual Studio 2022 with C++ desktop development, and the Windows SDK 10.0.26100 or newer. After cloning the repository recursively, a supplied Build.bat script locates the game files, checks for missing dependencies, and performs the compilation, placing results in a Documents\Leonida folder. The build can be paused and resumed, and the scripts support both Windows and Linux environments for certain components.

Overall, Leonida represents a technical foundation for running the Xbox version of GTA VI on PC without traditional emulation, preserving the user’s own copy of the game while reusing its assets and code. Although the project is still early and the game does not yet launch, the extensive shader translation, asset extraction, and Vulkan backend work demonstrate significant progress toward a functional PC port.

stories.author: alpaylan
stories.title: A Better Vocabulary for Testing
stories.groq_label: A more precise, actionable taxonomy for software testing—based on scope, statefulness, and method—replaces vague unit/integration/E2E terms and guides test selection
stories.groq_explain:
The article argues that the terminology used to discuss software testing is vague and insufficient. It points out that common labels such as “unit,” “integration,” and “end‑to‑end” do not clearly define what is being tested, how it is tested, or the resources required. The author observes that classifications for stress, load, and penetration testing are also loosely applied, often based on “vibes” rather than a systematic framework.

To address this, the piece proposes a more precise and actionable vocabulary. The first dimension it introduces is the scope of a test, which is defined along two axes. The first axis is the programming‑language construct being exercised—function, class, module, or whole system. The second axis distinguishes whether the test targets a stateful or stateless entity. By separating these aspects, the author explains how inputs for functions (often arbitrary structures) differ from inputs for systems (typically serialized directives), and how state can be transformed into inputs to make testing more tractable.

The article then discusses how Design by Contract (DbC) and richer type systems can narrow the input space for functions, making tests more meaningful. An example is given where a hashmap lookup is theoretically fallible in the language but, in practice, should always succeed; DbC can capture such domain knowledge as contracts that can be checked at runtime or compile time.

The second major category is the purpose or hypothesis behind a test. Every test formulates a hypothesis that can be falsified. The author distinguishes domains such as functional correctness, performance (execution time), and security (resistance to attacks). For distributed systems, additional considerations include network latency, message loss, and hardware faults.

Although the article focuses particularly on random testing—a technique the author has been working on—it suggests that a clearer taxonomy would allow teams to upgrade or downgrade testing strategies based on available resources and to select appropriate methods for a given situation. By providing a more structured set of terms, the proposed vocabulary aims to make testing decisions more systematic, improve communication among developers, and ultimately lead to more reliable software.

stories.author: sebaandrada
stories.title: PcapAnalyzer – self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors
stories.groq_label: PcapAnalyzer is a self‑hosted PCAP analyzer that runs 27 detectors to quickly identify network problems
stories.groq_explain:
PcapAnalyzer is a self‑hosted tool that analyzes network capture files (pcap or pcapng, including gzipped versions) to quickly identify faults in a network. It runs locally on the user’s machine, ensuring that captured traffic never leaves the network, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license in a beta state. The application provides twenty‑seven built‑in detectors that examine different layers of network communication. These detectors cover TCP issues such as firewall blocks, retransmissions, duplicate acknowledgments, loss, reordering, window problems, resets, and slow handshakes; path problems including PMTUD black holes, low MSS, IP fragmentation, ICMP errors, and routing loops; name and address services like unanswered or slow DNS queries, DNS errors, DHCP failures, duplicate IPs, and ARP storms; application‑level problems such as HTTP error codes, slow responses, TLS alerts, and outdated SSL/TLS versions; tunnel anomalies for IPsec, WireGuard, OpenVPN, GRE, L2TP and Teredo; and security concerns such as port scans, cleartext credential transmissions, Telnet, SMBv1, SNMP v1‑v2c, ARP spoofing, and overlapping IP fragments.

The tool also evaluates capture quality, warning when the capture itself limits the analysis, for example when frames are duplicated, traffic is seen only in one direction, packets are truncated, or connections were already open at the start of the capture. The user interface offers Wireshark‑style views with packet lists, filter support, colour coding, CSV export, expert information, tables for HTTP, DNS, DHCP and TLS, response‑time metrics and flow diagrams for each conversation.

An optional AI investigation can be enabled by supplying the user’s own Anthropic API key. The AI runs the same analysis, cites the specific packets that support each finding, and can answer follow‑up questions. A demo mode provides the full analysis without an API key, generating text from the analysis at no cost. Results can be exported as PDF reports and the interface is available in both English and Spanish with light and dark themes.

PcapAnalyzer can be started quickly using Docker and Docker Compose, which creates a random access token for the local web service. For users who prefer not to use Docker, the backend can be run with Python 3.9+ and the frontend with Node 20+, requiring tshark from Wireshark. The application listens only on localhost and must be protected by an authenticated reverse proxy if exposed to a network, because the API can access the AI account.

Privacy is emphasized: the capture is processed locally, the AI sees only encrypted metadata unless the user explicitly enables packet‑content analysis, and all data are deleted after the AI session or after a period of inactivity. No telemetry, accounts, or third‑party data collection are performed in the self‑hosted version.

The repository includes tests, a quick‑start guide, feedback instructions, and references to a technical JSON schema in Spanish. The software is free to download, with a free version hosted on Gumroad, and a live demo is available online. It matters because it enables network engineers and security analysts to diagnose problems in seconds rather than hours while keeping sensitive traffic data under their control.

stories.author: vasie
stories.title: Pandex – Official European Law for AI Agents, over MCP
stories.groq_label: Pandex provides a unified API and searchable database of EU and European national laws and court rulings for AI agents.
stories.groq_explain:
Pandex is a platform that provides official European legal documents, including national legislation, historical law versions, and highest-court rulings, formatted specifically for software applications and artificial intelligence agents. It aggregates primary legal texts straight from issuing authorities across the European Union, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Austria, Switzerland, Luxembourg, and the Council of Europe, with additional European countries planned for future inclusion. By unifying diverse legal systems into a single schema, the service replaces the need to write separate web scrapers for every court and jurisdiction.

The platform interfaces with existing AI development tools and provides access through a REST API and a Model Context Protocol server. It supports keyword, semantic, and hybrid search across languages, enabling users to query in one language and retrieve exact matching legal passages published in another. For compliance and legal research, Pandex tracks legislative history by maintaining past versions of legal articles alongside their effective dates, allowing software to ground answers in verified law with complete citation links.

Pandex currently manages millions of official documents, court decisions, legislative acts, searchable passages, and cross-referenced citations. It provides transparent coverage statistics for every tracked institution, explicitly reporting which legal archives are complete and noting where technical limitations, such as external bot protections or delay periods, temporarily affect full data collection.

Access to the platform starts with a free tier during its beta period, allowing up to one thousand requests per day. Commercial plans include a pay-as-you-go API option based on request volume, a founding customer program offering fixed pricing and source prioritization, and a direct feed subscription that delivers raw legal files and daily change updates for local system indexing. Pandex provides developers with a structured, reliable source of official legal data necessary for building accurate AI legal research, compliance, and monitoring tools.

stories.author: f311a
stories.title: Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396)
stories.groq_label: Ghostscript use after free in the Type 1 font loader (CVE 2026 125396) permits sandbox escape and remote command execution across numerous services.
stories.groq_explain:
Upload2Shell (CVE‑2026‑125396) is a critical remote‑code‑execution vulnerability discovered in Ghostscript’s Type 1 font loader. The flaw is a use‑after‑free that allows a crafted document to break out of Ghostscript’s ‑dSAFER sandbox, modify native path controls and run attacker‑chosen commands inside the rendering process. Because Ghostscript is commonly invoked by print, email, upload and preview pipelines, the vulnerability can be reached through many downstream services.

The researchers first identified a path out of the ‑dSAFER boundary on 27 July 2026. By 30 July they demonstrated that a signed‑out request for a malicious file could reach Ghostscript in Google’s document rendering pipeline, and they supplied a production‑grade proof to Google. In August WordPress Core was shown to expose the renderer to users with Author privileges and to Contributors granted the upload_files capability, leading to a separate fix (CVE‑2026‑65640). The upstream Artifex bug tracker received a report (Bug 709684) on 2 September, and a Ghostscript release (10.08.0) was made available by 9 September.

Further production‑level findings were confirmed in other services. A Dropbox document‑processing route, Debian’s CUPS IPP service, Roundcube’s thumbnail generation, Plesk Obsidian’s Roundcube integration, the Essential Addons for Elementor widget, Forminator’s PDF form handling, Mayan EDMS’s document inbox, DokuWiki’s ImageMagick backend, MediaWiki’s PdfHandler, and ResourceSpace’s preview worker all exhibited remote command execution when processing malicious inputs that passed through Ghostscript. Each vendor was contacted in mid‑September and the reports were logged with timestamps.

Debian published a security update for Ghostscript in its unstable branch on 12 September, followed by a Debian 13 security update on 25 September. The same month Debian Security released a stable‑security update (10.05.1~dfsg‑1+deb13u3) marking the issue fixed. Ubuntu’s USN‑8949‑1 on 21 October incorporated the Ghostscript fix for seven Ubuntu releases, including Pro and Legacy branches. Roundcube released a hardening update on 19 October to restrict unsafe image types before ImageMagick conversion (CVE‑2026‑114727). Google mitigated its production path on 9 November, and a CVE identifier was assigned on 9 November, with the public CVE‑2026‑125396 entry published on 10 November.

The timeline concludes with an ongoing “rolling publication” of case studies, proofs and vendor responses, and a note that any additional print filters, thumbnailers or document preview components that invoke Ghostscript could become future attack vectors. The vulnerability matters because it provides pre‑authentication remote code execution across a wide array of widely deployed services, potentially compromising servers running Debian, Ubuntu, Google Cloud, WordPress sites, email platforms and many open‑source web applications. The coordinated disclosure and rapid patching across the ecosystem illustrate the broad impact of a single low‑level flaw in a foundational image‑processing library.

stories.author: k__
stories.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory
stories.groq_label: LookAtMyQuant compresses Inkling-2-Mini to 5.4 GB at 1.63 bits per weight while preserving most of its performance.
stories.groq_explain:
The page describes LookAtMyQuant, a quantization compiler that evaluates the impact of compressing each stored element of a model on its output and selects coding schemes so the entire model fits a size budget with minimal degradation. The tool is released under the MIT license and the methods and results are documented on the site.

LookAtMyQuant 2 is demonstrated on several models. For Qwen3.5‑4B it reduces the model to 1.23 GB, about 2.3 bits per weight, while still solving 330 of 540 exact‑answer math problems. This is comparable to Prism ML’s Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B, which solves 328 problems at a similar size, but the original Qwen3.5‑4B solves 359. The KL divergence of the quantized model on held‑out text is 0.45 nats versus 0.59 for Bonsai. The approach combines post‑training quantization with trellis codes, calibration on the model’s own math solutions (giving digit tokens ten times more weight), Fisher‑information‑based bit allocation per row, and 4 000 steps of distillation where each layer is re‑quantized once from the original weights. The entire process costs roughly $34 of GPU time. The resulting 1.23 GB file is packaged for the Apple Silicon runtime.

Applying the same recipe to Qwen3.8‑27B compresses it from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB (2.1 bits per weight) while retaining full performance on the 540 math benchmark (401 correct answers) and surpassing a competing Unsloth GGUF of the same size on HumanEval, MMLU and GSM8K. A 4‑bit DSpine drafter (1.02 GB) is also provided, which roughly doubles decode speed on math and code on Apple silicon.

The section titled “Inkling‑2‑Mini in 5.4 GB and 8.9 GB” details the compression of the 26.4 B physical / 5.4 B active 3‑times‑looped mixture‑of‑experts model from thinkingmachines/Inkling‑2‑Mini. Using the same compiler and a proximal fine‑tuning method (SQYFR), the model is reduced to 5.38 GB (1.63 bits per weight) and to 8.87 GB (2.69 bits per weight). Compression employs 4 KB SRAM hashed block‑vector trellis codes, row trellis codes, and a floor on the tail language‑model head bucket. Evaluations against the BF16 teacher model on GSM8K (200 test items) and HumanEval (164 problems) show that the 5.38 GB version achieves 134 correct GSM8K answers (67 % of the teacher) and 60 correct HumanEval solutions (36.6 %). The 8.87 GB version matches the teacher on GSM8K with 148 correct answers (74 %) and improves KL divergence compared with several Unsloth GGUF variants. At 5.38 GB the model outperforms a 9.14 GB Unsloth model on both GSM8K and HumanEval while being 41 % smaller. At 8.87 GB it matches the BF16 teacher on GSM8K and reduces KL by more than twofold on English/chat/code and by 29.6 % across 13 languages relative to the Unsloth baseline.

Performance on Apple silicon is reported for both compressed sizes. The 5.4 GB model decodes at about 73 tokens per second serially and a median of 125 tokens per second, with higher rates for math, reasoning and code, and a prefill speed of roughly 1 037 tokens per second using 5.83 GB of RAM. The 8.9 GB model decodes at about 63 tokens per second serially and a median of 101 tokens per second, with a prefill speed of 838 tokens per second using 9.32 GB RAM.

Installation instructions are provided for Apple silicon: installing the runtime package via pip from the GitHub repository, which brings in mlx, mlx‑lm, numpy and huggingface‑hub without needing PyTorch. The lamq command line tool can generate or chat with any supported model, optionally using a drafter, and accepts various flags for prompt handling, temperature, mode, and output format. The page also shows how to load a model programmatically with the runtime_mlx Python module, returning a model and tokenizer compatible with mlx_lm generation functions.

Overall, the page presents a quantization framework that achieves substantial size reductions for large language models while preserving or even improving task performance, and offers ready‑to‑use Apple silicon binaries and tooling for developers.

stories.author: andsoitis
stories.title: Jensen Huang's fall is bad news for Silicon Valley's accelerationists
stories.groq_label: Jensen Huang's setback undermines the drive for rapid tech advancement in Silicon Valley
stories.groq_explain: The article’s title, “Jensen Huang’s fall is bad news for Silicon Valley’s accelerationists,” suggests that it examines the consequences of a setback experienced by Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, for a group of technologists and investors who champion rapid, disruptive innovation—often referred to as accelerationists. The piece likely outlines how Huang’s decline, perhaps in terms of personal reputation, corporate performance, or strategic missteps, undermines the optimism and momentum that accelerationists rely on to push forward breakthrough technologies such as artificial intelligence, advanced graphics processing, and related hardware. It probably argues that Huang’s influence has been a rallying point for the belief that the industry can sustain exponential growth, and his fall therefore dampens enthusiasm, slows investment, and may prompt a re‑evaluation of the aggressive growth narratives that dominate Silicon Valley. The article would explore why this matters: a weakened champion could affect funding cycles, alter the strategic direction of startups, and temper the broader confidence in the sector’s ability to drive rapid technological change. In sum, the piece appears to discuss the broader ripple effects of a high‑profile leader’s troubles on the culture and economics of fast‑paced innovation in the tech hub.
